title: PRD — Hot-route capacity protection (Hosted API + Dedicated): tier semantics, customer experience, and rollout
creator: Nikhil Sharma
body:
## Summary
Hot-route capacity protection introduces tier-aware quotas/rate limits and priority routing/admission control for Redwood Inference’s highest-traffic, highest-SLA API routes (initial MVP focus: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/rerank). The intent is to prevent fleet-wide degradation caused by overload on a small set of routes and workload shapes (“noisy neighbor” / hot-route cascades), while keeping customer behavior predictable, debuggable, and supportable.

This PRD defines:
- Customer-facing tier semantics (enterprise vs best-effort)
- What customers will see during overload (429s, headers, reason codes, streaming termination)
- How priority is determined and what is explicitly NOT promised
- Success metrics + guardrails
- Rollout plan (canary/GA), documentation, and comms requirements

## Background / Problem
We have seen incidents where a burst on a single high-traffic route (commonly chat) or a single tenant with long prompts drives queue depth and tail latency up across shared GPU pools, resulting in:
- Enterprise customers missing latency/availability commitments
- Elevated 5xx / timeouts for unrelated workloads
- On-call thrash due to ambiguous signals (is it quota? overload? runtime issues?)

The core product gap: we do not have explicit, enforceable tier semantics for “who gets served first” under pressure, and we do not provide deterministic/transparent overload behavior.

## Goals
1) Protect fleet health
- Avoid fleet-wide tail-latency cascades and 5xx spikes due to overload on a small number of hot routes.

2) Guarantee enterprise behavior (within defined semantics)
- Introduce explicit priority classes and per-route budgets that preserve enterprise SLO behavior during regional/fleet pressure.

3) Make overload behavior observable and supportable
- Clear 429 semantics, reason codes, and metrics so Support/CS/on-call can quickly explain and troubleshoot.

4) Minimize developer surprise
- Consistent status codes, payloads, and headers; documented retry/backoff guidance; clear escalation path for exceptions.

## Non-goals (explicit)
- No dynamic pricing changes. Billing changes limited to metadata/hooks (e.g., reason code attribution) to support later analysis.
- No fairness-scheduler rewrite. We integrate with existing scheduler and add signals/admission controls.
- No promise of “zero 429s” for enterprise. The promise is bounded: prioritized admission up to route/tier budgets + deterministic degradation when exceeding budgets or in severe capacity loss.
- No silent quality changes: fallback only where explicitly allowed and communicated (see Fallback Policy Guardrails).

## Definitions / Scope
### “Protected routes” (MVP)
Routes that receive prioritized admission control and dedicated observability/SLO views:
- /v1/chat/completions
- /v1/embeddings
- /v1/rerank

We may expand based on traffic/incident learnings (e.g., /v1/responses or internal compatibility endpoints) but MVP must ship with the above.

### Tiers / Priority classes (customer-visible semantics)
We will align to existing packaging language as much as possible while making the behavior enforceable.

1) Enterprise Priority (contracted / SLA-backed)
- Eligible workloads: accounts on enterprise plans and allowlisted as “priority-enabled” for protected routes.
- Behavior under pressure: admitted ahead of best-effort traffic; protected by per-route budgets and overload thresholds.
- Expected outcome: enterprise traffic should maintain published SLO targets for protected routes during moderate overload; in severe capacity loss, enterprise may still see throttling but later than best-effort and with explicit reason codes.

2) Best-effort (self-serve and non-priority traffic)
- Behavior under pressure: throttled earlier and more predictably; may experience 429s during bursts or when regional capacity is constrained.
- Expected outcome: clear, consistent throttling semantics; stable error rates (avoid 5xx/timeouts when we can shed with 429 instead).

### How priority is determined
Priority is determined by:
- Account tier (enterprise vs self-serve)
- Route group classification (protected vs standard)
- Region policy and capacity signals (queue depth, scheduler lag, saturation)
- Optional customer-specific overrides (approved exceptions only)

Priority does NOT depend on model choice alone. (Some models may have different effective capacity; that is a routing implementation detail and not a customer-facing guarantee.)

## Customer Experience Requirements
### 429 response semantics (standard)
When requests are not admitted due to quota/rate limit or overload shedding, the API must return HTTP 429 with:
- Stable JSON error envelope (no HTML, no variant payloads across gateway/routing)
- A machine-readable reason code and human-readable message
- Retry guidance via headers

Required headers (names finalized with Eng; this PRD defines intent):
- Retry-After: seconds (when applicable)
- X-Redwood-RateLimit-Limit / Remaining / Reset (for quota/rate limit evaluation)
- X-Redwood-Overload-Reason (when shedding due to overload)
- X-Redwood-Tier (observed/evaluated tier for this request)
- X-Redwood-Route-Group (protected vs standard)

Reason code taxonomy (customer-visible)
We will document a small set of stable reason codes. MVP:
- quota_exceeded: request rejected because customer exceeded quota window
- rate_limited: request rejected due to per-second (or short-window) rate limits
- overload_shed: request rejected due to overload protection / admission control under pressure
- capacity_unavailable: request rejected due to severe capacity loss where no fallback is allowed

Messaging requirements
- Error message must be explicit about whether the customer should retry, backoff, or contact support.
- We must avoid implying “bug” or “server error” for overload_shed. The correct framing: “capacity protection is active; retry with backoff.”

### Streaming behavior requirements
For streaming responses (chat/completions), if shedding occurs before first token:
- Return a standard 429 response (no partial stream)

If shedding occurs mid-stream (rare; should be minimized by admission control):
- Terminate the stream with a consistent, documented final event indicating termination reason, plus a request id that Support can use.
- Never terminate with ambiguous TCP resets as the primary/expected mode.

### Fallback policy guardrails (enterprise-safe)
Fallback is a powerful lever but high risk for silent quality changes. We will only allow fallback where we can enforce:
- Contractual allowance (some enterprise accounts may require strict model/region pinning)
- Model-compatibility and safety checks (tokenizer, tool-calling/JSON mode capabilities)

Customer-facing rule:
- If customer pins a specific model version (or uses a “strict” enterprise policy), we prefer admission control (429) over silent fallback.
- For non-strict policies, we may fallback to a compatible model variant/region during overload, but must:
  - Emit explicit headers/telemetry identifying the fallback
  - Document which endpoints may fallback and how to detect it

### Console / transparency (internal first, customer later)
MVP requirements (internal operator view):
- Display tier limits and recent overload events per route group
- Show breakdown of 429 reason codes by tier and route

Customer-facing transparency (not required for MVP GA):
- Post-GA candidate feature: show “throttling events” with reason codes in customer dashboard.

## Product Requirements
### Tier semantics + defaults
- Define tier-by-route defaults (limits/budgets) that meet enterprise SLO targets without starving fleet.
- Defaults must be conservative and adjustable via config.
- Customer-specific exceptions require an approval workflow and must be time-bounded (see Exceptions).

### Predictability requirements
- Consistent 429 payload schema across all regions.
- Idempotent quota evaluation (same inputs => same decision); decision logs should be explainable for enterprise escalations.
- “Fail closed” vs “fail open”:
  - For enterprise priority: prefer fail-open to preserve service when policy engine is degraded, but do not allow uncontrolled overload. Proposed compromise: cache last-known-good policy for a bounded time.
  - For best-effort: fail-closed is acceptable if policy evaluation is unavailable (to protect fleet).

### Observability requirements (customer-impacting)
- Per-route/per-tier dashboards for:
  - Request rate, admitted vs rejected
  - 429s by reason code
  - p50/p95/p99 latency and error rates (2xx/4xx/5xx)
  - Queue depth / scheduler lag signals that drive protection
- Explicit “overload protection activated” annotations for incident timelines.

## Success Metrics (acceptance criteria)
Primary (enterprise protection)
- During simulated overload on a protected route, enterprise tier maintains:
  - p95 latency within SLO target for the route in the canary region
  - 5xx rate does not increase above defined burn thresholds
- Enterprise 429 rate increases are bounded and attributable (overload_shed vs quota) with clear reason code distribution.

Primary (fleet health)
- Under overload, we see a decrease in fleet-wide 5xx/timeouts compared to baseline incidents (replace “unbounded retries + timeouts” with controlled 429 shedding).
- No cascading queue growth across unrelated route groups.

Secondary (supportability)
- Support can identify root cause of a 429 within 5 minutes using reason codes + dashboards.
- Reduce incident time-to-mitigation for hot-route bursts (measured via on-call timelines).

Guardrails
- No meaningful regression in median latency attributable to policy evaluation overhead (target: <1ms additional overhead at gateway/routing for steady state; final number owned by Eng but tracked here as a product constraint).
- No new high-cardinality metric explosions (must conform to metrics standards).

## Rollout Plan
### Phases
1) Internal + staging validation
- Validate headers/payload schema; ensure SDKs and popular client patterns handle 429/Retry-After correctly.

2) Canary (single region; allowlisted enterprise accounts)
- Start in us-east
- Route scope: protected routes only
- Tier scope: enterprise allowlist + best-effort baseline
- Go/no-go gates:
  - Enterprise SLO burn not worse than baseline
  - 429 reason code distribution matches expectation
  - No dashboard/metric integrity issues

3) Multi-region expansion
- Expand to eu-west next; tune thresholds per region capacity signals.

4) GA enablement
- Enable for all protected routes and all enterprise accounts (subject to policy constraints), with documented exception workflow.

### Rollback
- Feature flags by region and route group
- Fast rollback path: disable admission control enforcement and revert to legacy throttling for best-effort if needed (last resort; must be tested)

## Exceptions / Escalation Policy
Exception types
- Temporary burst allowance increase
- Route group custom budget adjustment
- “Strict pinning” (no fallback) enforcement

Process
- All exceptions require:
  - TAM/CS request + documented customer justification
  - SRE + Platform review for fleet risk
  - Time-bound TTL and re-evaluation date
  - Audit trail (ticket + config change link)

## Documentation + Comms Requirements
Docs (required for GA)
- Public docs: 429 reason codes, headers, retry/backoff guidance, and tier semantics at a high level
- Support docs: macro language for quota vs overload_shed; when to escalate
- Runbook link in internal tooling for on-call

Customer comms
- Enterprise email/announcement framing: “capacity protections to improve stability on peak usage”
- Avoid language that implies “paid customers will always be served.” Use language consistent with SLOs and budgeted capacity.

## Open Questions
- Final naming: do we use “Priority routing” vs “Capacity protection” publicly? Product preference: “capacity protection” externally; “priority classes” internally.
- What is the minimal customer-visible tier taxonomy we can support long-term without frequent renames?
- Should we expose tier classification headers to all customers by default, or only in debug mode?

## Linked Work
- Design/ADR/specs: see Confluence ADR on enforcement points and technical design doc (links maintained in ENG-4921 epic).
- Engineering tickets: ENG-4922 (gateway limiter), ENG-4923 (policy engine), ENG-4924 (routing signals), ENG-4926 (dashboards), ENG-4930 (support playbook).

## Decision Log (high level)
- We will standardize on 429 for quota/rate limit + overload shedding (not 503) to drive predictable client behavior and reduce retries/timeouts.
- We will not allow silent fallback for strict enterprise policies; where fallback is allowed, it must be detectable and documented.
- Rollout will be region-by-region with allowlists and explicit monitoring gates.
